topics.title: Start with the observed disagreement
topics.summary: A wrong result, a resource failure, and a slow result call for different first questions. When the value is wrong, reduce the input while preserving the failure and compare the public contract with the observed output. When an allocation fails, inspect the accepted size and ownership transition. When elapsed time is high, establish that the result is correct before interpreting performance. Changing a representation without identifying the violated requirement can hide one symptom while creating another.

blocks.text: A useful incident record contains the input, expected property, actual observation, build configuration, source revision, and the smallest known reproduction. “The tree fails sometimes” is not a reproduction. “After inserting 4,2,6,5 and deleting 4, inorder traversal contains 4 again” identifies an operation history that can be traced through the ownership links.

topics.title: Use operation histories, not only snapshots
topics.summary: Many data-structure defects need a sequence of actions. A tombstone bug requires insertion, collision, deletion, and a later lookup or update. A tail-pointer bug may require removing the only node and then inserting another. A circular buffer defect may appear only after several wraparounds with alternating full and empty states.

blocks.text: Represent these histories as replayable operations. Save the random seed and the actual minimized sequence when a generated test fails. A seed alone is not always a durable reproduction across changes to the generator or its operation distribution. Keep the operation grammar small enough that the sequence can be read and edited by a person.

blocks.headingContext: Use operation histories, not only snapshots

blocks.text: After each action, check both the return value and a structural observation. For a map, compare all visible key/value associations, not just the most recent key. For a queue, compare size and logical order. For a search tree, compare membership and inorder contents, while recognizing that a valid inorder list alone does not prove height metadata or parent links.

topics.title: Distinguish missing results from exceptional failures
topics.summary: An unsuccessful search is often an ordinary result. An invalid vertex index is a rejected request. Exhausted memory is an environmental failure. Treating all three as the same empty return value prevents callers from choosing an appropriate response.

The application does not reinterpret disconnection as a parser failure merely because no route can be produced.

topics.chapterTitle: Appendix A — An Algorithmic Diagnostic Desk Reference
topics.title: Keep four forms of evidence separate
topics.summary: A proof explains why a stated algorithm satisfies a property under assumptions. A reference comparison checks agreement with another implementation. A sanitizer run investigates exercised low-level behavior. A benchmark records performance for a specified workload and environment. A strong engineering argument often uses all four, but none automatically replaces the others.

blocks.text: For example, an invariant can establish that lower-bound search shrinks the interval correctly. Exhaustive small-vector tests can catch an implementation typo. Sanitizers can expose an out-of-bounds access in an executed path. A benchmark can compare repeated query costs after sorting. Reporting one of these as all four exaggerates what was established.

topics.title: Decide whether to keep a custom structure
topics.summary: A custom teaching implementation makes hidden mechanisms visible. That is a learning benefit, not a reason to deploy it by default. Before replacing a standard container, write down the required operation mix, size range, ownership constraints, iterator guarantees, failure behavior, and measured bottleneck. Include maintenance and verification costs in the decision.

blocks.headingContext: Decide whether to keep a custom structure

blocks.text: A fixed-capacity specialized queue may be appropriate when rejecting overflow is part of the protocol. A hand-written general tree may be inappropriate when its deletion, allocator behavior, exception guarantees, and long-term maintenance are unproven. The choice should follow requirements and evidence rather than the amount of code already invested.
